lead: An ideal solution is a useful reference for liquid mixtures. It says each component's fugacity is proportional to its mole fraction at fixed temperature and pressure. The proportionality constant is the fugacity of the pure component. This simple rule, called the Lewis-Randall rule, gives Raoult's law at low pressure and lets you calculate vapour compositions without activity coefficients. Real mixtures deviate from it; the sign and size of the deviation tell you whether the components like each other more or less than they like themselves. Refineries, distilleries and solvent plants use this reference daily.
prereq: You need: chemical potential, fugacity, and ideal-gas mixtures from Unit 2 (see Unit 2, Ideal gas and ideal-gas processes).

blocks.text: An ideal solution is a model for a liquid mixture in which the chemical potential of every component follows one simple equation. At fixed temperature T and pressure P:

blocks.where: μ<sub>i</sub> is the chemical potential of component i in the solution (J/mol); μ<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> is its chemical potential as a pure liquid at the same T and P; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is temperature in K; x<sub>i</sub> is its mole fraction.

blocks.text: The standard state μipure is the pure liquid at the same T and P, not at 1 bar and not the ideal gas. When xi = 1, ln xi = 0 and μi = μipure, so the equation returns the pure liquid. The model assumes molecules of similar size and similar intermolecular forces, mixed randomly. It does not assume zero forces. The forces still exist; the energy of unlike contacts is taken as the average of like contacts. Therefore an ideal solution has zero enthalpy of mixing, ΔHmix = 0, and zero volume change on mixing, ΔVmix = 0. Its entropy of mixing is the same as for ideal gases, ΔSmix = −R Σ xi ln xi. This definition is a reference, not a law of nature. See Chapter 5.1 for the meaning of μ.

Lewis and Randall extended the pure-component fugacity to mixtures. For an ideal solution, f<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup>. Here f<sub>i</sub> is the fugacity of component i in the solution (kPa); f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> is the fugacity of pure liquid i at the same T and P; x<sub>i</sub> is the liquid mole fraction. This is the Lewis-Randall rule. At low pressure, f<sub>i</sub> ≈ p<sub>i</sub> and f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> ≈ P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, so the rule becomes p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, which is Raoult's law. p<sub>i</sub> is the partial pressure (kPa), and P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is the vapour pressure of pure i at T (kPa). For two components, P = p<sub>1</sub> + p<sub>2</sub> = x<sub>1</sub>P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> + (1−x<sub>1</sub>)P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup>, a straight line in x<sub>1</sub>. The bubble-pressure line plots this P against liquid x<sub>1</sub>; the dew curve plots P against vapour y<sub>1</sub>. The vapour mole fraction is y<sub>i</sub> = p<sub>i</sub>/P. Compare this with an ideal-gas mixture: there f<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>P and the standard state is the ideal gas at 1 bar. An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces; an ideal solution has forces but no net change on mixing. Same word ideal, different physics.

Real liquid mixtures disobey the rule. If pi is greater than xiPisat, the mixture shows positive deviation from Raoult's law. The activity coefficient γi = ai/xi is greater than 1. The unlike molecules attract each other less than like molecules, so each component escapes more easily. Ethanol + water is a common example. If pi is less than xiPisat, the deviation is negative and γi < 1: the unlike molecules attract each other more strongly than like molecules, so each component escapes less easily (chloroform + acetone is a common example; such systems can form a maximum-boiling azeotrope). As xi → 0, Raoult's law fails for that component even when the solvent still follows it; Henry's law replaces it: pi = Hixi, where Hi is Henry's constant in kPa, found from data at the same T. Hi is not Pisat. The standard state for the solvent is the pure liquid, the Lewis-Randall choice. The standard state for a dilute solute is Henry's hypothetical pure liquid, obtained by extrapolating Henry's law to xi = 1. The general non-ideal form is fi = xiγifipure. Activity and γ are developed in Chapter 5.7.

figure.caption: Bubble pressure rises as a straight line; dew pressure is curved. At P = 58 kPa the bubble point is x₁ = 0.30 and the dew point is y₁ = 0.517.

spec.aria: A pressure-composition diagram: bubble pressure 40 + 60x₁, dew pressure 1/(y₁/100 + (1−y₁)/40). At 58 kPa the bubble point is x₁ = 0.30 and the dew point is y₁ = 0.517; the two curves meet at the pure ends, 40 kPa and 100 kPa.

examples.question: At 350 K, pure liquid 1 has P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 100 kPa and pure liquid 2 has P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 40 kPa. The liquid is ideal and contains x<sub>1</sub> = 0.30. Find the partial pressures p<sub>1</sub> and p<sub>2</sub>, the total pressure P, and the vapour mole fraction y<sub>1</sub>. State any assumption.
steps: For an ideal solution at low pressure, Raoult's law gives p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>.
y<sub>1</sub> = p<sub>1</sub>/P = 30/58 = 0.5172. Also y<sub>2</sub> = 28/58 = 0.4828, and y<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>2</sub> = 1.
Assumption: the vapour is ideal and the pressure is low enough to neglect fugacity corrections.
examples.answer: p<sub>1</sub> = 30 kPa, p<sub>2</sub> = 28 kPa, P = 58 kPa and y<sub>1</sub> = 0.5172.
examples.check:
p1 = 0.30 * 100
p2 = (1 - 0.30) * 40
P = p1 + p2
y1 = p1 / P
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(P)
print(round(y1, 4))

traps: Confusing an ideal solution with an ideal gas. An ideal solution has ΔH<sub>mix</sub> = 0 and ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 0; it does not have zero intermolecular forces.
Using Raoult's law for a dilute solute. When x<sub>i</sub> is small, Henry's law p<sub>i</sub> = H<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub> is the correct limit, and H<sub>i</sub> is not P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>.

Mixing liquid and vapour mole fractions. In p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, x<sub>i</sub> is the liquid composition; in y<sub>i</sub> = p<sub>i</sub>/P, y<sub>i</sub> is the vapour composition.
Taking the standard state as pure liquid at 1 bar. The Lewis-Randall standard state is pure liquid at the same T and P as the solution.

Setting f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> equal to P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> at high pressure. At low pressure they are close; at high pressure f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> must include the fugacity coefficient.

quiz.q: State the Lewis-Randall rule for f<sub>i</sub> in an ideal solution.
quiz.a: f<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub>f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup>, where f<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> is the fugacity of pure component i at the same T and P.

quiz.q: Why does an ideal solution have zero enthalpy of mixing even though molecules attract?
quiz.a: Unlike contacts have the average energy of like contacts, so breaking like contacts and forming unlike contacts gives no net energy change. Forces exist; their net mixing effect is zero.

quiz.q: At 300 K, P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 80 kPa and P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup> = 50 kPa. An ideal liquid has x<sub>1</sub> = 0.20. Find P and y<sub>1</sub>.
A mixture has p<sub>1</sub> greater than x<sub>1</sub>P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> at x<sub>1</sub> = 0.5. What is the sign of γ<sub>1</sub> and what does it say about unlike interactions?
quiz.a: γ<sub>1</sub> > 1, so the deviation is positive. Unlike interactions are weaker than like interactions, so component 1 escapes more easily than in an ideal solution.

quiz.q: Why is Henry's constant H<sub>i</sub> not equal to P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>?
quiz.a: Henry's law applies at infinite dilution, where each solute molecule is surrounded by solvent. H<sub>i</sub> depends on solute-solvent interactions and T, not on the vapour pressure of pure solute.

quiz.q: At T and P, f<sub>1</sub><sup>pure</sup> = 120 kPa and f<sub>2</sub><sup>pure</sup> = 60 kPa. The solution is ideal with x<sub>1</sub> = 0.25. Find f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub>.
At low pressure, is the bubble-pressure curve of an ideal solution always a straight line in x<sub>1</sub>? Explain.
quiz.a: Yes, if both P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> are constant at fixed T. Then P = x<sub>1</sub>P<sub>1</sub><sup>sat</sup> + (1−x<sub>1</sub>)P<sub>2</sub><sup>sat</sup>, which is linear in x<sub>1</sub>. The dew curve is not linear.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators store pure-component vapour pressures and Henry constants, then switch between Lewis-Randall and Henry standard states depending on composition. Distillation columns use the same bubble and dew curves, but with activity coefficient models when the liquid is non-ideal. Electrolyte solutions and polymer solutions need their own standard states because Henry's law alone is not enough. Search for gamma-phi formulation, Henry standard state and VLE data regression.
